metadata.title: Three Witnesses to Two Per Second
metadata.subtitle: the qualifier that falls off
metadata.presenter: Tanmay Kulkarni, in for Humanitarians AI

beats.narration_text: Two per second. A room of people tapping a finger at whatever speed feels natural. A stranger walking down a street, measured through the top of their head. The stressed syllables in an English sentence. Three measurements, three fields that do not cite each other, and the same number.

legibility.artifact: Three spectra stacked, drawn one per sentence: tap intervals, head acceleration, speech envelope. Each carries its own citation line beneath it, legible as that measurement is named - van Noorden & Moelants (1999); MacDougall & Moore (2005); He et al. (2024). A single vertical rule at 2 Hz lands across all three on the last line and holds. No branding, no title, no logo anywhere in this beat.

beats.narration_text: This is Tanmay Kulkarni in for Humanitarians AI. That number gets used to argue that human beings run on one shared internal clock. I went and read the three studies underneath it. Two of them hold. The third one never said what it gets quoted as saying.

legibility.artifact: Title card: Three Witnesses to Two Per Second. Presenter line beneath.

beats.narration_text: Witness three. Speech carries a nested rhythm. Syllables run in the theta range, roughly four to eight hertz, and the sources disagree inside that window. Underneath the syllables, the stress beat runs at about half that rate. Two hertz.

legibility.artifact: Nested rhythm diagram: syllable band drawn as a range, not a point, with both disagreeing source ranges labelled (4-5 Hz and 5-8 Hz) and cited separately. Stress beat at 2 Hz beneath.

beats.narration_text: I am going to show you two sentences. Here is the one in the research. The rhythm of the stress foot in English is centred around two hertz. And here is how it usually comes back to you. Speech runs on a two hertz beat. One of those says less than the other. Find it before I say it.

legibility.artifact: Both sentences on screen together, full width, source above and retelling below, with the citation under the source. After the narration ends the frame holds in silence for 2 s with no highlight, no arrow and no motion - the viewer is finding it. This is the only silent hold in the film.

beats.edit_note: Parent audio TRIMMED at a detected pause (2.70s), removing the first two sentences -- 'Question three. What qualifier sits in the original.' -- which dangle without B02. No audio was regenerated and no word was rewritten: this is the signed take with a head trim, so the parent Gate P signature still covers every word heard.
beats.silence_note: Added silence is 1.36s, not 2.0s. This beat's own audio ends with 0.64s of silence, so 2.0 added measured 2.62s of dead air against a design of two seconds. The number here is ADDED silence; perceived hold is this plus the tail.

beats.narration_text: In English. Two words. They are sitting in the source, and they are gone from the retelling. And with them goes the difference between a fact about people and a fact about a language.

legibility.artifact: The two words isolate and hold in the source sentence; the same position in the retelling below stays visibly empty. Both remain on screen together.

beats.narration_text: Somebody went and checked. Thirty four listeners. Seventeen native English speakers, seventeen native Mandarin speakers, listening to speech built at stress rates of one, two, and three hertz. Brain to speech tracking peaked at two hertz for the English speakers. For the Mandarin speakers, that peak was absent.

legibility.artifact: Two tracking curves plotted on one axis, English and Mandarin, with the 2 Hz point marked on both. Drawn simultaneously, not sequentially, and held. Citation: He, Buder & Bidelman (2024), Brain and Language 256:105463.

beats.narration_text: Your turn, and it is a measurement, not a search. Tap a finger for thirty seconds at whatever feels natural, and count them. If you land at ninety, or a hundred and forty, you have not broken the model. You have found the spread that one number hides. Then take any claim that separate fields independently agree on something, go to the original sentence, and look for the qualifier. Three Witnesses to Two Per Second. Tanmay Kulkarni, in for Humanitarians AI, signing off.

legibility.artifact: A thirty-second counter runs on screen while the instruction is spoken, so the viewer can start immediately. The observed spread is shown as a strip beside it - 54 to 170 with 90 and 140 marked, the two numbers the narration names - rather than re-staging the full witness-one scatter, which would repeat a frame the viewer already read.
End card: title, a pointer to the full 4:52 film and what it holds that the Short does not, presenter, channel handle.
